vignette:
**Patient Vignette: "Raj" (Age 49, South Asian Male, Military Medic)**

Raj presents as a lean, composed man whose posture—shoulders squared, hands resting flat on his knees—betrays decades of military discipline. He speaks in a measured, deliberate cadence, as if still triaging his words for urgency. He is a medic with twenty-three years of service, currently stationed at a large base where he runs trauma training for new recruits. He has been married to his wife, Priya, for twenty-two years. They have two children, a daughter in college and a son in high school.

The event that reshaped Raj’s life occurred fourteen months ago, on a Thursday evening. He had returned home late from a 72-hour shift, exhausted, his body still vibrating with the adrenaline of a mass-casualty drill. Priya was waiting in the kitchen. There had been tension for months—arguments about money, about his absences, about her feeling invisible. That night, she was crying. He tried to put a hand on her shoulder. She shoved him. He remembers the shock more than the pain. Then she slapped him. Then she began hitting his chest, his arms, his face, screaming that he was never there, that she was drowning alone.

Raj did not fight back. He was trained to de-escalate, to protect the vulnerable. He stood still, arms at his sides, and took it. He did not raise his voice. When she stopped, breathless and shaking, he went to the garage and slept in his car. He did not tell anyone. He did not report it. He told himself it was a single moment of stress, that she was not herself, that he could absorb this the way he absorbed everything else—by compartmentalizing it, by locking it in a steel box in his chest.

But the box has rusted through.

In the months since, Raj has become a ghost in his own home. He avoids the kitchen at night. He flinches when Priya reaches for him, even to hand him a cup of tea. He has stopped sleeping in their bed. He now sleeps on a cot in the basement, surrounded by old gear and boxes of medical supplies. He tells himself it is because he snores, or because he needs to be near his equipment for early drills. But the truth is that he cannot close his eyes without seeing her face contorted with rage, without feeling the thud of her fists against his ribs. He has nightmares—not of combat, but of her. In the dreams, she is holding a knife. In the dreams, he is a child again, small and helpless. He wakes gasping, his hands up in a defensive posture he learned in basic training.

At work, Raj is functional but brittle. He still runs his trauma simulations with precision, but his patience is gone. A recruit’s slow tourniquet application once made him scream—a full-throated, guttural roar that silenced the entire hangar. He apologized immediately, but the look on the young soldier’s face stays with him. He has started drinking after shifts. Just two beers, then three. He tells himself it is to sleep. He knows it is to forget.

He has not told his commanding officer. He has not told his children. He has not told his brother, who lives three hours away. The shame is a physical weight in his gut—a dense, hot stone. He is a medic. He is supposed to save people. He is supposed to be strong. How could he, a man who has treated battlefield wounds, be broken by his own wife? He replays the night constantly, searching for what he did wrong. He thinks: *If I had been a better husband. If I had come home earlier. If I had not been so tired.* The self-blame is a loop, and he cannot step off it.

He no longer goes to the grocery store alone. He avoids crowded places. He has stopped answering phone calls from friends. He feels a constant, low-grade vigilance, as if danger is always just behind him. He checks the locks on the basement door three times before he lies down. He has started carrying a small folding knife in his pocket—something he never did before, even in combat zones.

When asked how he is, Raj says, "Fine." He says it with a tight smile. He says it so often that he almost believes it. But his hands tremble when he talks about the future. He cannot imagine next year. He cannot imagine next month. He lives in a narrow, gray present, waiting for the next blow—even though Priya has never hit him again. Even though she has apologized, begged him to talk to her, cried in the doorway of the basement. He cannot trust her. He cannot trust anyone. The person who was supposed to keep him safe became the danger.

He is still a medic. He still saves lives. But he cannot save his own.
